This trigger looks clinically disconnected from the stated trauma context and the rest of the network.

'I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. In an older married male refugee with severe PTSD symptoms, self-harm can occur, but here it is the only extreme behavioral regulation item and is unsupported by the other selected strategies, memories, or appraisals. It appears clinically out of pattern relative to the otherwise avoidance/vigilance-focused presentation.

vignette:
Prem, at 75, carried the quiet stillness of a man whose hands had shaped clay for decades, but beneath that calm surface, an old storm raged. His journey to America had been one of desperate flight as a young man, caught in the brutal upheaval of displacement in his homeland. He could not put the frightening events into words, not truly. Instead, his memory of that time was a collection of disconnected pieces that never quite fit into a coherent narrative. He would recall the acrid smell of burning fields, the stifling heat of an overcrowded truck, the terrified whimpers of a child, and the sight of a small, hastily dug grave by the roadside. These fragments, unlike any ordinary memory, felt more real, more vivid, as if they were happening right now, the sensations still sharp decades later.

The trauma had etched itself into his daily existence. The sudden blare of a car horn or the squeal of tires on the road outside his pottery studio could instantly transport him back to the frantic escape, the constant fear of pursuit. His heart would pound, his breath catch, and his hands, usually so steady on the wheel, would tremble uncontrollably. He had come to believe he had to be especially careful because you never knew what could happen next, a deep-seated certainty that kept him in a state of constant vigilance. This meant that even in the familiar comfort of his studio, surrounded by his creations, he would constantly scan his environment for any signs of threat, his eyes darting to the windows, his ears straining for unusual sounds.

His once vibrant social life had dwindled significantly. Prem found himself increasingly avoiding situations that might make him feel happy or hopeful. Invitations to family celebrations, especially weddings or birth announcements, were politely declined, not because he didn't care, but because the surge of positive emotion felt foreign, almost dangerous, a vulnerability he couldn't afford. The thought of attending a funeral or visiting a cemetery filled him with a profound dread, not just of grief, but of the raw, visceral memories of loss and unmarked graves that would inevitably resurface. He would make excuses, feeling a deep pang of regret, yet certain it was for the best to protect himself from the overwhelming feelings.

His artistic output, once a source of immense pride, had also changed. He still worked, meticulously shaping clay, but the joy had faded. He found himself sticking to simpler forms, avoiding the intricate, ambitious pieces that used to define his skill, believing deep down that he was no longer capable of doing the things that truly defined him as an artist. This conviction was reinforced by his perceived inability to deal with even the slightest upset. A minor flaw in a pot, a small disagreement with his wife, or a delayed supply order would send him into a spiral of self-doubt and anxious rumination, confirming his belief that his coping reserves were utterly depleted.

This pervasive sense of fragility and the need for control permeated his marriage to his wife, Kamala. She had tried to talk to him about his withdrawal, his increasing quietness, but he would quickly shut down any potential disagreement. He had learned to avoid conflict at all costs, fearing that even a small argument could unravel his fragile composure, proving his appraisal of "low coping" correct. Kamala, seeing his distress, had gently but firmly encouraged him to seek help. It was her quiet persistence, combined with a recent, particularly vivid flashback triggered by seeing a police car on their street – a fleeting image that brought back the terror of uniformed figures from his past – that finally spurred Prem to acknowledge that he could no longer manage this alone. He came to therapy, not with hope, but with a weary resignation, primarily because he couldn't bear to see the worry in his wife's eyes any longer, and a quiet, desperate wish for some respite from the storm within.
